summary.text: A free module is a module that has a basis, meaning a generating set that is linearly independent.
Every vector space is a free module, but when the coefficient ring is not a division ring, non-free modules exist.
Given any set S and ring R, there is a free R-module with basis S, called the module of formal R-linear combinations of the elements of S.

facts.label: A ring over itself
facts.value: It is a free module of rank one

facts.label: Basis of the ring
facts.value: Any unit element works as a basis

facts.label: Direct sums
facts.value: A direct sum of free modules is free

facts.label: Whitehead problem
facts.value: Whether a Whitehead group is free is independent of ZFC

facts.label: Over the integers
facts.value: For finitely generated modules, free, projective, flat and torsion-free coincide

items.prompt: You are working with vector spaces over a field, and someone asks what they are in the language of modules. What is the answer?

options.label: Every vector space is a free module
Every vector space is a non-free module
Only some vector spaces are modules at all
A vector space is a module only over the integers

items.explain: Every vector space is a free module, since it has a basis.

items.prompt: The coefficients now come from a ring that is not a division ring. What can happen to a module over it?

options.label: Every module still has a basis
Some modules can fail to be free
Bases become unique for every module

items.explain: If the coefficient ring is not a division ring, there exist non-free modules; over a field this cannot happen.

items.prompt: Treat a ring R as a module over itself. Which element can serve as a basis?
items.explain: A ring is a free module of rank one over itself, and any unit element is a basis.

items.prompt: You combine free modules in two ways: by a direct sum, or by an infinite product. Which combination is guaranteed to stay free?

options.label: The infinite product, but not the direct sum
The direct sum, but not generally the infinite product

items.explain: A direct sum of free modules is free, while an infinite cartesian product of free modules is generally not free.

items.prompt: A finitely generated module over the integers is known to be torsion-free. What follows?

options.label: It could still fail to be free

items.explain: For a finitely generated module over a principal ideal domain such as the integers, free, projective, flat and torsion-free are equivalent.

items.prompt: A famous question asks whether a certain kind of group, a Whitehead group, is free. What is its status?

options.label: The standard axioms of set theory cannot settle it

items.explain: Whether a module is free is sometimes undecidable in the set-theoretic sense; the Whitehead problem turned out to be independent of ZFC.
